meta.description: Ted Williams gets the credit and no one contests it — but no date, game or page was ever attached. The trail ends at a 1982 quote anthology.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'They invented the All-Star game for Willie Mays'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Ted Williams everywhere, sourced nowhere: Quote Investigator has no article, Wikiquote files it unsourced, and the oldest printing found is 1982.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder, 19-time All-Star
answer.sourceLine: Every printing credits Ted Williams, no one else has ever been proposed, and the sentiment sits comfortably with a man who was a 19-time All-Star himself. But no speech, interview, column, broadcast or book page has ever been attached to it: Quote Investigator has no article on it ↗, English Wikiquote keeps it off the article entirely, and the oldest printing we could locate is a 1982 quotation anthology that supplies no source of its own.

source.excerpt: They invented the All-Star game for Willie Mays.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ has never taken this line on. A search of the site for Willie Mays returns two hits — its piece on Tallulah Bankhead’s “two geniuses” remark and a Jesse Owens quotation that mentions Mays in passing — and nothing on this line, so there is no specialist finding to defer to, and nothing here contradicts one.
English Wikiquote does not carry the quotation in its Ted Williams article ↗ at all. It sits instead on the article’s talk page ↗, in a list headed “Unsourced.”

Simple English Wikiquote ↗ does file it under “Sourced quotes,” but the reference is Baseball Almanac’s Ted Williams quotations page — and that page ↗ gives the line a source field of its own reading “Widely Attributed,” on a page where other entries name books and magazines.

A full-text sweep of the Internet Archive’s scanned books returns nineteen printings ↗ — quotation anthologies, trivia books, devotionals, team histories and one novel. The oldest is Kevin Nelson’s Baseball’s Greatest Quotes, published by Simon and Schuster in 1982 ↗, and it too gives only “—Ted Williams.”
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller passage to show. In fifteen of the nineteen printings located in the Internet Archive’s scanned book corpus the line stands alone as a single free-standing sentence, introduced by some variant of “Ted Williams once said” and followed by the author’s own commentary; the remaining four are an almanac page, a calendar entry, a devotional and a novel. Not one of the nineteen follows it with a date, a game, or a citation.

source.rightsNote: Because the origin of the wording is undetermined, no copyright status can honestly be asserted here. If Williams did say it, it was a short spoken remark of unknown date and setting; what we can point to is the printings, and those are in copyright — the earliest located, Kevin Nelson’s Baseball’s Greatest Quotes (Simon and Schuster, 1982) ↗, along with every later anthology that repeats it.

author.name: Ted Williams
author.heading: Who was Ted Williams?
author.metaLine: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder · Hall of Fame, 1966
author.bio: Ted Williams played his whole major-league career in left field for the Boston Red Sox — 1939 to 1942 and 1946 to 1960, with the gap carved out by military service — and finished with a .344 lifetime batting average. He was selected to 19 All-Star teams and went into the Hall of Fame on the first ballot in 1966. He knew the occasion intimately: of his walk-off home run in the 1941 All-Star Game he later said it “remains to this day the most thrilling hit of my life.” Which is part of why a one-line compliment about someone else owning that same stage sounds so much like him.

misattribution.heading: Not a wrong name — a missing source
misattribution.intro: This is not the usual case of a line pinned on the wrong famous person. Nobody has ever credited it to anyone but Ted Williams. What has gone wrong is the paperwork: a citation chain that loops back on itself, a bare aggregator entry treated as evidence, and a novel that gets read as a source.

items.why: Lists the line under “Sourced quotes,” which reads as a verification. The footnote points to a Baseball Almanac quotations page — see the reference for yourself ↗. English Wikiquote reaches the opposite conclusion and keeps the line off the article altogether, listing it on its talk page under “Unsourced” ↗.

Prints “They invented the All-Star Game for Willie Mays.” — Ted Williams with no date, game or publication, on a page where neighbouring quotations do carry sources ↗, one of them credited to Charles Einstein in The Fireside Book of Baseball (1956). The site sources what it can; it does not source this.

Eugena Pilek's novel has a character say “Ted Williams said ‘they invented the all-star game for Willie Mays.’” It surfaces in full-text book searches ↗ alongside the non-fiction hits, and gets picked up as a book citation complete with a page number. A novel repeating a floating quotation is not provenance.

The phrasing wobbles in exactly the way orally transmitted lines do. Across the scanned printings ↗ you find “All-Star Game-for Willie Mays” and a split between capital “Game” and lower-case “game”; widen the search by one word ↗ and a version turns up that drops Mays’s surname altogether and ends at “for Willie.” No fixed text is being copied — a remembered sentence is.

misattribution.truthLine: No one has ever credited this sentence to anybody but Ted Williams — and no one has ever recorded where he said it. Until someone produces a game story, a column, a transcript or a page, “attributed” is the honest label. See every printing we could find ↗.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: It is one of the shortest and largest compliments in baseball. Not he was great in All-Star Games — the whole institution existed as a stage for one man. And the numbers do not embarrass it: the Baseball Hall of Fame calls Willie Mays a 24-time All-Star ↗ who won the game's MVP award in 1963 and again in 1968, and he still holds or shares the career All-Star marks for at bats, runs, hits, total bases, triples and extra-base hits ↗.

It also sounds right coming from Ted Williams, which is exactly the property that lets a quotation travel without papers. Williams was a 19-time All-Star with his own claim on the game's history, and his Red Sox career ended after the 1960 season while Mays kept turning up in All-Star line-ups into the 1970s — so the remark reads as something said looking back, not something said in the moment. That is as far as the evidence goes. Nearly every book that repeats it introduces it the same way: Ted Williams once said. None of them says when, where, or to whom.
detailsBody: A full-text search of the Internet Archive's scanned book corpus for the exact phrase returns nineteen books. Reading every snippet: fifteen introduce it with some form of “Ted Williams once said,” one is a page of a quotation almanac, one is a daily-thought calendar entry, one is a devotional, and one is a novel in which a character quotes it. Not one is a biography of Mays or of Williams, and not one carries a citation.

There is a single exception worth flagging honestly. John Rosengren's Hammerin’ Hank, George Almighty and the Say Hey Kid (2008) is the only book in that set that attaches an endnote marker to the sentence. The scan is lending-restricted and we could not open the note, so we do not know what it cites — it remains the most promising lead anyone with library access could chase.
context.pull: The compliment is perfect. The paper trail is empty.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator has no article on "They invented the All-Star game for Willie Mays". A site search for Willie Mays returns exactly two results: the Tallulah Bankhead "two geniuses" piece and "Quote Origin: Find the Good. It's All Around You...", a Jesse Owens quotation whose article names Mays only as an exemplar Owens admired.
The line appears on Wikiquote's Talk:Ted Williams page in a list under the heading "Unsourced".
English Wikiquote's Ted Williams article does not contain the line at all (sections: Quotes, Quotes about Ted Williams, External links).

Simple English Wikiquote lists the quote under "Sourced quotes" with its only citation being reference [5], "Ted Williams Quotes", Baseball Almanac, baseball-almanac.com/quotes/quowilt.shtml (retrieved 2009-09-20) - not the All-Star Game quotes page.

Baseball Almanac's All-Star Game Quotes page prints "They invented the All-Star Game for Willie Mays." - Ted Williams with no source, while a neighbouring quotation is credited to Charles Einstein in The Fireside Book of Baseball (1956).

Baseball Almanac's Ted Williams Quotes page - the page Simple English Wikiquote actually cites - prints the line with a Source field reading "Widely Attributed", while other entries on the same page name sources such as The 2006 ESPN Baseball Encyclopedia, My Turn at Bat, The Sporting News (04/25/1994) and Sports Illustrated (08/08/1966).

A full-text search of the Internet Archive book corpus for the exact phrase returns 19 results, all secondary compilations with bare attribution, including Eugena Pilek's novel Cooperstown, Dan Fost's Giants Past & Present, Les Krantz's Reel Baseball ("All-Star Game-for Willie Mays"), and John Rosengren's book where the line carries endnote marker 14. Fost's full snippet reads "...All-Star Game for Willie Mays.\" Indeed, Mays played in 22 All-Star Games as a Giant (and two as a Met)..." - 22 + 2 = 24, matching the Hall of Fame figure, so Fost's count is correct.

Widening the full-text search by one word (dropping "Mays") returns about 20 results and surfaces the surname-dropped variant "They invented the All-Star Game for Willie." in Jason Grasso's Measuring Up to the Ohio Learning Outcomes, a title not among the nineteen printings of the full phrase.
Kevin Nelson's Baseball's Greatest Quotes: The Wit, Wisdom, and Wisecracks of America's National Pastime was published by Simon and Schuster in 1982.
Ted Williams was born in 1918, died 5 July 2002, played left field for the Boston Red Sox 1939-1942 and 1946-1960, was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 1966, and was a 19-time All-Star selection.

Ted Williams was born 30 August 1918 in San Diego, had a .344 career batting average, and said of his 1941 All-Star Game home run that it "remains to this day the most thrilling hit of my life"; the article does not mention Willie Mays.
The Baseball Hall of Fame describes Willie Mays as a 24-time All-Star who won the All-Star Game MVP in 1963 and 1968, was inducted in 1979, and died 18 June 2024.
Willie Mays holds or shares the career All-Star Game records for at bats (75), runs (20), hits (23), total bases (40), triples (3) and extra-base hits (8).
